\label{thm:main}
		For every $\varepsilon>0$ and every real $X\ge4$,

		|E(X)|\lesssim_\varepsilon X^{209/670+\varepsilon}.

		There are constants $c_1,c_2>0$ such that, for either sign and all
		sufficiently large $X$,
		\[
		c_1\mathcal L(X)\le\sup_{X\le x\le2X}(\pm E(x))
		\le c_2\mathcal L(X).
		\]

head: environment

label: eq:Vaaler
title: Proof
body_md:
For $t\in\mathbb R$, set $\psi(t)=t-\lfloor t\rfloor-1/2$, and fix
		a nonintegral $X\ge4$.
		The classical reduction \cite[proof of \mbox{\hyperlink{cite.GK}{Theorem~4.8}}]{GK}, followed by
		dyadic subdivision, expresses $E(X)$, up to $O(1)$, as a linear
		combination with coefficients $\pm4$ of $O(\log X)$ sums
		\[
		\sum_{n\in I\cap\mathbb Z}\psi\!\left(\frac XM F(n/M)\right),
		\qquad I\subseteq[M,2M],\quad 1\le M\le\sqrt X,
		\]
		where $I$ is an interval and $F$ is as in \eqref{eq:S}, with
		\[
		(\alpha,\kappa)\in
		\left\{\left(\pm\frac1{4M},0\right),
		\left(0,\pm\frac M{4X}\right)\right\}.
		\]
		Thus the four arguments are exactly $X/(4n\pm1)$ and
		$X/(4n)\pm1/4$. These are the four residue-class and sawtooth phases
		in the cited circle reduction. This identifies that standard reduction
		with the reciprocal family \eqref{eq:S} without adding a new analytic
		input. The pointwise Vaaler majorant applies to the convention
		$\psi(t)=\{t\}-1/2$ used here, including integral arguments.
		For any integer $J\ge2$, Vaaler's approximation
		\cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.Vaaler85}{Theorem~18}}]{Vaaler85} and partial summation in $h$ give
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:Vaaler}
			\begin{split}
				&\left|\sum_{n\in I\cap\mathbb Z}\psi\!\left(\frac XM F(n/M)\right)\right|\\
				&\quad\lesssim\frac MJ+
				\sum_{\substack{H=2^j<J\\j\ge0}}\frac1H
				\sup_{H\le H'\le\min(2H,J)}
				\left|\sum_{H\le h<H'}\sum_{n\in I\cap\mathbb Z}
				e\!\left(\frac{hX}{M}F(n/M)\right)\right|.
			\end{split}
		\end{equation}
		For $M\ge2X^\beta$, choose $J=\lfloor MX^{-\beta}\rfloor$.
		Then $J\ge2$, $M/J\lesssim X^\beta$, and every $H<J$ satisfies
		$H\le MX^{-\beta}$. \mbox{\hyperref[thm:recip]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:recip}}}, with $T=X$ and
		$g=G=1$, bounds each supremum in \eqref{eq:Vaaler} by
		$O_\varepsilon(HX^{\beta+\varepsilon})$. After multiplication by
		$H^{-1}$, each dyadic $h$-block therefore contributes
		$O_\varepsilon(X^{\beta+\varepsilon})$. There are only
		$O(\log X)$ such blocks. The dyadic $n$-blocks with
		$M<2X^\beta$ have total length
		$O(\sum_{M<2X^\beta}M)=O(X^\beta)$, so their contribution is
		trivial. Absorbing the logarithm into $X^\varepsilon$ proves the claim
		for nonintegral $X$. Finally, the counting function in the definition of
		$E(X)$ is right-continuous, hence so is $E(X)$. Letting a nonintegral
		argument decrease to an integral $X$ gives the same estimate there.

label: prop:preliminary

name: Classical bounds

title: Proof
body_md:
The exponent pairs $(k,l)=(2/7,4/7)$ and $(13/31,16/31)$
		\cite[Chapter~3, (3.3.4)]{GK} give, for every integer $h\approx H$
		and every interval $I\subseteq[M,2M]$,
		\[
		\left|\sum_{n\in I\cap\mathbb Z}e\!\left(\frac{hT}{4(n+M\alpha)}\right)\right|
		\lesssim (hT/M^2)^kM^l+\frac{M^2}{hT}.
		\]
		The constants are uniform in $\alpha$. Put
		$u=n+\lfloor M\alpha\rfloor$ and $a=\{M\alpha\}$. Then
		$n+M\alpha=u+a$, with $u\in\mathbb Z$, $u\eqsim M$ and $0\le a<1$.
		For real $x\eqsim M$ and integers $j\ge0$,
		\[
		\frac{d^j}{dx^j}(x+a)^{-2}
		=(-1)^j(j+1)!x^{-j-2}\bigl(1+O_j(M^{-1})\bigr).
		\]
		When $hT/M^2$ is bounded, the second-derivative test
		\cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.GK}{Theorem~2.2}}]{GK} gives the stronger bound $O(\sqrt M)$.
		If $M$ is bounded, both estimates in \eqref{eq:preliminary} follow
		from the trivial bound after enlarging the absolute constant, so we may
		assume $M$ is larger than a fixed constant. Since
		$\|G\|_\infty+\operatorname{Var}(G)\le1$, discrete Abel summation reduces the
		weighted $n$-sum to interval sums of the form just estimated, with no
		loss beyond an absolute constant. The same argument applies to an
		intersected dyadic interval. Finally, $|g|\le1$ and $h\approx H$, so
		summing these bounds over the $O(H)$ admissible integers $h$ and then
		dividing by $H$ gives \eqref{eq:preliminary}. To finish the parameter check,
		\[
		\frac{M^2}{HT}\le1,\qquad \frac{2(1+s)}7=\beta,\qquad
		\frac{13p+3m}{31}\le\frac{1293}{4154}<\beta
		\quad(p\le42/67).
		\]

label: eq:sqrt-phase
title: Proof
body_md:
For $h,q>0$, set $f_h(q)=\sqrt{Thq}-\omega q$. For each integer
		$h\approx H$, let $c_h\in\mathbb C$ and let $I_h\subseteq[U/100,2U]$
		be an interval. Define
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:sqrt-phase}
			\mathcal S=\sup_{|c_h|\le1,\ I_h\subseteq[U/100,2U]}
			\left|\sum_{h\approx H}c_h\sum_{q\in I_h\cap\mathbb Z}e(f_h(q))\right|,
		\end{equation}
		where the supremum is over these coefficient and interval families.
		Abel summation and the van der Corput
		formula \cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.Huxley96}{Lemma~5.5.3}}]{Huxley96} give
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:reciprocal-transfer}
			\frac{|S|}{H}\lesssim\frac{M}{H\sqrt\rho}\mathcal S
			+\log(2+U)+\frac{M}{\sqrt\rho}.
		\end{equation}
		Here the inversion formula is applied on the actual subinterval of the
		$n$-sum. Its endpoint-uniform error is the displayed
		$O(M/\sqrt\rho+\log(2+U))$. The derivative check below gives
		$|\phi_h''|\eqsim\rho/M^2$ and a dual frequency interval of length
		$O(U)$, which are precisely the scales entering that error term. If an
		endpoint derivative is integral, changing the half-weight convention
		costs $O(M/\sqrt\rho)$ and is already absorbed by the same error.
		For $h>0$ and $x>-M\alpha$, define
		$\phi_h(x)=hT/[4(x+M\alpha)]$. For $q>0$, let $x_{h,q}$ be the
		unique solution of $\phi_h'(x_{h,q})=-q$. Then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:reciprocal-stationary}
			\begin{gathered}
				x_{h,q}=\frac{\sqrt{hT}}{2\sqrt q}-M\alpha,\qquad
				\phi_h(x_{h,q})+qx_{h,q}=f_h(q),\\
				(\phi_h''(x_{h,q}))^{-1/2}
				=\frac{(hT)^{1/4}}{2q^{3/4}}
				=\frac{M}{2\sqrt\rho}(h/H)^{1/4}(q/U)^{-3/4}.
			\end{gathered}
		\end{equation}
		For $h\approx H$ and $x\in[M,2M]$, these frequencies lie in $[U/100,2U]$.
		$\phi_h''\eqsim\rho/M^2$ and
		$|\phi_h^{(j)}|\lesssim\rho M^{-j}$ for $j=3,4$.
		The factor $(q/U)^{-3/4}$ has uniformly bounded variation on
		$[U/100,2U]$. Apply
		\eqref{eq:abel-bv} to it and to $G$. The remaining factors have bounded
		modulus and are absorbed in $c_h$. This proves
		\eqref{eq:reciprocal-transfer}, uniformly on the stated intervals.
		
		We next prove
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:average-mixed}
			\mathcal S\lesssim_\varepsilon T^\varepsilon
			\left[HJ+\left(\frac{\rho J^6}{U^6}\right)^{1/30}
			(HU)^{14/15}B^{1/30}\right].
		\end{equation}
		The choice of $J$ and \eqref{c:middle-region} imply
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:shift-checks}
			\begin{gathered}
				J\ge T^{5/134},\qquad J/U=(MJ)/\rho\lesssim T^{-6/67},\\
				\rho(J/U)^7=(MJ)^7/\rho^6\lesssim1,\qquad
				\rho J^6/U^6=(MJ)^6/\rho^5\ge T^{1/67},\\
				\rho/U^5=M^5/\rho^4\le T^{-1/134}.
			\end{gathered}
		\end{equation}
		Averaging over integer shifts $1\le r\le J$ changes each interval sum by
		$O(J)$. Define the Taylor remainder $R_{h,q}$ by
		\[
		f_h(q+r)=f_h(q)+\sum_{i=1}^6A_i(h,q)r^i+R_{h,q}(r)
		\qquad(0\le r\le J).
		\]
		Taylor's formula gives
		\[
		\sup_{\substack{(h,q)\in\Omega\\0\le r\le J}}|\partial_rR_{h,q}(r)|
		\lesssim\frac{\rho J^6}{U^7}\lesssim J^{-1}.
		\]
		For $b_{h,q}(r)=e(R_{h,q}(r))$, therefore,
		\[
		\sup_{(h,q)\in\Omega}|b_{h,q}(J)|+
		\sum_{r=1}^{J-1}\sup_{(h,q)\in\Omega}|b_{h,q}(r+1)-b_{h,q}(r)|\lesssim1.
		\]
		By \eqref{eq:abel-bv}, it suffices to bound, for every integer
		$1\le j\le J$ and every complex family $(d_{h,q})_{(h,q)\in\Omega}$
		with $|d_{h,q}|\le1$,
		\[
		\sum_{(h,q)\in\Omega}d_{h,q}
		\sum_{r=1}^j e\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^6A_i(h,q)r^i\right).
		\]
		For complex coefficients $d_1,\ldots,d_J$ and
		$y=(y_1,\ldots,y_5)\in\mathbb T^5$, the degree-five Vinogradov mean value
		theorem \cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.BDG}{Theorem~1.1}}]{BDG}, by expansion and orthogonality, gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:VMVT}
			\sup_{|d_r|\le1}\int_{\mathbb T^5}
			\left|\sum_{r=1}^Jd_r e\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^5y_ir^i\right)\right|^{30}dy
			\lesssim_\varepsilon J^{15+\varepsilon}.
		\end{equation}
		Indeed, expansion of the left side leaves only the degree-five Vinogradov
		system. Every surviving coefficient product has modulus at most one, so
		Theorem~1.1 of \cite{BDG} with $s=15$ and degree $5$ bounds the integral
		by $J_{15,5}(J)\lesssim_\varepsilon J^{15+\varepsilon}$.
		For a sufficiently large fixed $C\ge1$, apply
		\eqref{eq:elementary-sieve} with moment exponent $30$ and
		\[
		D_i=1/2\ (1\le i\le5),\qquad D_6=C\rho/U^6,\qquad
		E_i=J^i\ (1\le i\le6).
		\]
		For $(h,q)\in\Omega$, write $A_i=A_i(h,q)$. Use
		$A_i-\lfloor A_i+1/2\rfloor$ for the first five sieve coordinates
		and $A_6$ for the sixth.
		The sieve pair count is bounded by $B$: discard its first three
		restrictions and use $|A_5|\lesssim\rho/U^5=o(1)$, so that the
		fifth centered representative equals $A_5$.
		For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_6)\in\prod_{i=1}^6[-D_i,D_i]$, fix $x_6$
		and absorb its phase into $d_r$. Equation~\eqref{eq:VMVT} then gives
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
			P:=\prod_{i=1}^6(1+D_iE_i)\eqsim J^{15}\frac{\rho J^6}{U^6},\\
			\sup_{|d_r|\le1}\left\|\sum_{r=1}^j d_r
			e\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^6x_ir^i\right)\right\|_{L^{30}_\#(\prod_{i=1}^6[-D_i,D_i])}
			\lesssim_\varepsilon J^{1/2+\varepsilon}.
		\end{gathered}
		\]
		The sieve bound, divided by $J$, is the second term of
		\eqref{eq:average-mixed}. Abel summation above and the $O(HJ)$
		endpoint error prove that estimate. Finally, the thirtieth power of
		the resulting main term in \eqref{eq:reciprocal-transfer} is
		\[
		\left[\frac{M}{H\sqrt\rho}
		\left(\frac{\rho J^6}{U^6}\right)^{1/30}
		(HU)^{14/15}B^{1/30}\right]^{30}
		=T\rho^8(MJ)^6\frac B{HU},
		\]
		using $U=\rho/M$ and $\rho^2=THU$.
		The other terms are bounded by those in \eqref{eq:pair-reduction}.

name: Proof of \Propref{prop:second

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $Q=2^jR$ with $j\ge0$ and $R\le Q\le c_*H$.
		The case $S_Q=0$ is immediate. Otherwise fix a rectangle attaining
		the maximum. For a sufficiently large fixed
		constant $C$, choose the box widths in \eqref{eq:distributional-sieve} as
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
			D=(NR^2/Q^3)^{1/2},\qquad
			(D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4)=C(1,1,D,D),\\
			(E_1,E_2,E_3,E_4)=C(KL,L,L\sqrt K,L/\sqrt K).
		\end{gathered}
		\]
		Write $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_4)\in\mathcal X=\prod_{i=1}^4[-D_i,D_i]$
		for the integration variable. Then $t_I\eqsim D$, and the four products have sizes
		\[
		(D_iE_i)_{i=1}^4\eqsim
		\left(\frac{NHQ^2}{R^4},\frac{HQ}{R^2},
		\frac{NH}{R^2},\frac HQ\right).
		\]
		They are bounded below by fixed positive constants, so
		\[
		P:=\prod_{i=1}^4(1+D_iE_i)\eqsim\frac{H^4N^2Q^2}{R^8}.
		\]
		The first two sieve restrictions give the corresponding conditions in
		\eqref{eq:pairs}. The other two imply
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\left|\frac{\gamma_{I'}d_{I'}^3}{\gamma_Id_I^3}-1\right|
			&\lesssim\frac{|t_I-t_{I'}|}{D}
			\lesssim\frac1{DL\sqrt K}\eqsim\frac{R^2}{HN},\\
			|\kappa_I-\kappa_{I'}|
			&\lesssim\frac{|\kappa_It_I-\kappa_{I'}t_{I'}|}{D}
			+\frac{|t_I-t_{I'}|}{D}\\
			&\lesssim\frac{\sqrt K}{LD}+\frac1{DL\sqrt K}
			\lesssim\frac QH.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Thus the sieve pair count is $O(B_Q)$, by \eqref{eq:pair-comparison}.
		
		The cone hypotheses follow from
		\[
		L\gtrsim W\to\infty,\qquad K/L\eqsim N/H\to\infty,\qquad
		\eta K\eqsim C_\eta Q/H,\qquad
		\eta KL\eqsim C_\eta(Q/R)^2.
		\]
		The preceding choices of $C_\eta$ and $c_*$ ensure
		$1\le L<K\le\eta^{-1}\le KL$. Also
		$D\eqsim(\eta L\sqrt K)^{-1}$. After interchanging the first two
		coordinates, cover their box and the third-coordinate interval by a
		bounded number of translates of a box with side lengths
		$2,2,2(\eta L\sqrt K)^{-1}$. Translation multiplies the coefficients
		by constants of modulus one. At each fixed fourth coordinate $x_4$,
		absorb $e(x_4l/\sqrt k)$ into those coefficients.
		\mbox{\hyperref[thm:first]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:first}}}, followed by integration in $x_4$, gives
		the distribution hypothesis of \mbox{\hyperref[lem:elementary-sieve]{Lemma~\ref*{lem:elementary-sieve}}}
		with constants $c_q\lesssim_\varepsilon T^\varepsilon\mathcal E_q^q$
		for $q\in\{4,6\}$.
		Hence \eqref{eq:Farey} and \eqref{eq:classical-spacing} give
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-Q-mixed}
			\begin{aligned}
				S_Q&\lesssim_\varepsilon T^\varepsilon\frac{R^2}{Q}
				\sum_{q\in\{4,6\}}P^{1/q}(\#\mathcal I_Q)^{1-2/q}B_Q^{1/q}\mathcal E_q\\
				&\lesssim_\varepsilon T^\varepsilon\frac{MR}{N}
				\sum_{q\in\{4,6\}}(R/Q)^{3-20/(3q)}W^{4/(3q)}\mathcal E_q.
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		More explicitly,
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
			\mathcal E_6\eqsim\frac{\sqrt{NH}}R\frac QR,\\
			\mathcal E_4\lesssim
			\frac{N^{1/4}H^{3/4}}R\frac QR
			+\frac{N^{1/2}H^{1/4}}{R^{3/4}}\left(\frac QR\right)^{5/4},
		\end{gathered}
		\]
		and therefore
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\frac{S_Q}{H}\lesssim_\varepsilon T^\varepsilon\bigg[
			&\frac{M}{\sqrt{HN}}W^{2/9}(R/Q)^{8/9}\\
			&+\frac{M}{N^{3/4}H^{1/4}}W^{1/3}(R/Q)^{1/3}\\
			&+\frac{MR^{1/4}}{N^{1/2}H^{3/4}}W^{1/3}(R/Q)^{1/12}\bigg].
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		For each $\delta>0$, $\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j\delta}=(1-2^{-\delta})^{-1}$.
		Sum the last display over $Q=2^jR$ and use
		\[
		\frac{MR^{1/4}}{N^{1/2}H^{3/4}}W^{1/3}
		=W^{-5/36}\frac{M}{\sqrt{HN}}W^{2/9},\qquad W\ge1.
		\]
		The error in \eqref{eq:class-reduction}, divided by $H$, is also
		bounded by the first term of \eqref{eq:second}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \mbox{\hyperref[lem:localization]{Lemma~\ref*{lem:localization}}} with loss $\delta>0$.
		Since $\#\mathcal P_\Delta\lesssim K/\Delta$,
		\[
		V^{-1}\sum_{\vartheta\in\mathcal P_\Delta}\|T_\vartheta\|_2^2
		\lesssim_\delta(KL)^\delta KL^2(\Delta+L+Z).
		\]
		For $\Delta<L+Z$, summing over $O(\log(2K))$ scales gives
		\[
		V^{-1}\sum_{\Delta<L+Z}\sum_{\vartheta\in\mathcal P_\Delta}
		\|T_\vartheta\|_2^2
		\lesssim_\delta(KL)^{2\delta}KL^2(L+Z).
		\]
		For $\Delta\ge L+Z$, a nonempty integration set in \eqref{eq:GMcone}
		requires
		\[
		c_\delta(KL)^{-\delta}\lambda^2\Delta^2/K^2
		\le\|T_\vartheta\|_\infty\lesssim\Delta L,
		\qquad
		\Delta\lesssim_\delta(KL)^\delta K^2L/\lambda^2.
		\]
		The geometric sum of these $\Delta$ is bounded by twice its largest
		term. Substitution in \eqref{eq:GMcone}, followed by
		\eqref{eq:cone-normalization}, yields
		\[
		\lambda^4\mathcal D(\lambda)
		\lesssim_\delta(KL)^{3\delta}
		\left(KL^2(L+Z)+\frac{K^3L^3}{\lambda^2}\right).
		\]
		Take $\delta=\varepsilon/4$.

name: Proof of \Thmref{thm:first

title: Proof
body_md:
For each finest sector $\theta$ and integers $k\approx K$, $l\approx L$,
		define $u_{\theta,kl}$ by
		\[
		\widehat u_{\theta,kl}(\xi)
		=\mathbf1_\theta(\xi)\widehat\chi\bigl(\xi-(l,kl,l\sqrt k)\bigr),
		\qquad f_\theta=\sum_{k\approx K,\,l\approx L}c_{kl}u_{\theta,kl}.
		\]
		Fourier inversion and Plancherel give
		\[
		\|u_{\theta,kl}\|_\infty\le\|\widehat\chi\|_1\lesssim1,\qquad
		\|u_{\theta,kl}\|_2\le\|\chi\|_2\lesssim V^{1/2},\qquad
		\|u_{\theta,kl}\|_4^4\lesssim V.
		\]
		
		Fix $\vartheta\in\mathcal P_\Delta$. Choose an interval in
		$[K,2K]$ of length $O(\Delta)$ containing every $k$ for which
		$u_{\theta,kl}\not\equiv0$ for some $\theta\subseteq\vartheta$ and $l\approx L$.
		Let $k_0$ be its midpoint, and put $t_0=\sqrt{k_0/K}$.
		Use the frequency coordinates
		\[
		(\zeta_1,\ \zeta_3-t_0\zeta_1,\
		\zeta_2-2t_0\zeta_3+t_0^2\zeta_1).
		\]
		The frequency $(l,kl,l\sqrt k)$ has coordinates
		\[
		\left(\frac lL,\frac lL(\sqrt{k/K}-t_0),
		\frac lL(\sqrt{k/K}-t_0)^2\right),
		\]
		and the widths of $B_\vartheta^*$ are comparable to
		$\eta/\sigma^2,\eta/\sigma,\eta$, where $\sigma=\Delta/K$.
		For $\theta\subseteq\vartheta$ and integers $k,k'\approx K$, $l,l'\approx L$,
		the condition
		$\psi_\vartheta*(u_{\theta,kl}\overline{u_{\theta,k'l'}})\not\equiv0$
		and \eqref{eq:cone-kernel} imply
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
			|l'-l|\lesssim LZ/\Delta^2,\\
			|l'(\sqrt{k'}-\sqrt{k_0})-l(\sqrt k-\sqrt{k_0})|
			\lesssim LZ/(\Delta\sqrt K).
		\end{gathered}
		\]
		The widths of $\widehat\chi$ are absorbed because $\eta KL\ge1$ and
		$\sigma\le1$. As $l'\eqsim L$ and
		$|\sqrt k-\sqrt{k_0}|\lesssim\Delta/\sqrt K$,
		\[
		\frac{L|k'-k|}{\sqrt K}
		\lesssim\frac{LZ}{\Delta\sqrt K}
		+\frac{LZ}{\Delta^2}\frac\Delta{\sqrt K}
		\lesssim\frac{LZ}{\Delta\sqrt K}.
		\]
		Thus
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:unrounded-pairs}
			|k'-k|\lesssim Z/\Delta,\qquad |l'-l|\lesssim LZ/\Delta^2.
		\end{equation}
		
		Each translated support meets $O(1)$ finest sectors. For a fixed
		$(k,l)$, \eqref{eq:unrounded-pairs} allows at most
		$C(1+Z/\Delta)(1+LZ/\Delta^2)$ choices of $(k',l')$.
		Since there are $O(\Delta L)$ choices of $(k,l)$,
		\[
		\|T_\vartheta\|_\infty
		\lesssim\Delta L(1+Z/\Delta)(1+LZ/\Delta^2)
		\lesssim\Delta L\qquad(\Delta\ge L+Z).
		\]
		This proves \eqref{eq:coarse-energy}.
		
		For every pair of projected summands, Young's and H\"older's
		inequalities give
		\[
		\|\psi_\vartheta*(u_{\theta,kl}\overline{u_{\theta,k'l'}})\|_2
		\le\|u_{\theta,kl}\|_4\|u_{\theta,k'l'}\|_4\lesssim V^{1/2}.
		\]
		Each term in the expansion of $\int_{\mathbb R^3}T_\vartheta(x)^2\,dx$
		is therefore $O(V)$. In a nonzero term, the integers $k_i,k_i'$
		lie in the fixed interval for $\vartheta$, and $l_i,l_i'\approx L$
		for $i=1,2$. Fourier support gives
		\[
		\left|\sum_{i=1}^2(l_i'-l_i)\right|\le4c_0/K<1,\qquad
		\left|\sum_{i=1}^2(k_i'l_i'-k_il_i)\right|\le4c_0<1.
		\]
		Both sums vanish. Define
		$d_i=k_i'-k_i$ for $i=1,2$, and $v=l_1'-l_1$. Then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:paired}
			l_2'-l_2=-v,\qquad
			l_1d_1+l_2d_2=v(k_2'-k_1'),\qquad
			|d_i|\lesssim Z/\Delta\quad(i=1,2).
		\end{equation}
		For this upper bound, discard the $l$-difference restriction in
		\eqref{eq:unrounded-pairs}.
		
		If $(d_1,d_2)\ne(0,0)$, interchange the two pairs so that $d_1\ne0$.
		Choose $k_1',k_2',v,d_2,l_2$ first. The number of choices is
		\[
		O(\Delta^2)\,O(L)\,O(1+Z/\Delta)\,O(L)
		=O\bigl(\Delta^2L^2(1+Z/\Delta)\bigr).
		\]
		For an admissible choice, the nonzero integer
		$D=v(k_2'-k_1')-l_2d_2$ satisfies
		\[
		l_1d_1=D,\qquad
		0<|D|=|l_1d_1|\lesssim L(1+Z/\Delta)\lesssim KL.
		\]
		The divisor bound \cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.HW}{Theorem~315}}]{HW} gives
		$O_\varepsilon((KL)^\varepsilon)$ choices of $(l_1,d_1)$.
		All remaining indices are determined by
		\[
		k_i=k_i'-d_i\quad(i=1,2),\qquad
		l_1'=l_1+v,\qquad l_2'=l_2-v.
		\]
		If $d_1=d_2=0$, \eqref{eq:paired} reduces to
		$v(k_2'-k_1')=0$. The cases $v=0$ and $v\ne0$ give, respectively,
		\[
		O(\Delta^2L^2),\qquad O(\Delta L^3).
		\]
		Consequently
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			V^{-1}\|T_\vartheta\|_2^2
			&\lesssim_\varepsilon(KL)^\varepsilon
			\bigl(\Delta^2L^2(1+Z/\Delta)+\Delta L^3\bigr)\\
			&=(KL)^\varepsilon\Delta L^2(\Delta+L+Z),
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		which is \eqref{eq:envelope-counts}.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $c:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, define
		\[
		N_c=\#c(\Omega),\qquad
		r_c(\nu)=\#\{t\in c(\Omega):t<c(\nu)\}.
		\]
		For an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, define
		$A_J=\{r_c(\nu):\nu\in\Omega,\ c(\nu)\in J\}$. This is a possibly empty interval
		of integers in $\{0,\ldots,N_c-1\}$. For $0\le j<N_c$, set
		$\gamma_J(j)=N_c^{-1}\sum_{v\in A_J}e(-jv/N_c)$.
		Finite Fourier inversion and summation of a geometric progression give
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
			\mathbf1_J(c(\nu))=
			\sum_{j=0}^{N_c-1}\gamma_J(j)e(jr_c(\nu)/N_c),\\
			|\gamma_J(j)|\lesssim\frac1{1+\min(j,N_c-j)},\qquad
			\sum_{j=0}^{N_c-1}\sup_J|\gamma_J(j)|\lesssim\log(2N_c).
		\end{gathered}
		\]
		Apply this to $c_1,c_2$ and multiply. Repeated values have the same
		rank, and all endpoint conventions are retained.

label: lem:elementary-sieve
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:elementary-sieve}
		Let $d,n\in\mathbb N$, let $D_i,E_i>0$ for $1\le i\le d$, and let
		$\mathcal I$ be finite. Suppose
		$x_j=(x_{j,1},\ldots,x_{j,d})\in\mathcal X=\prod_{i=1}^d[-D_i,D_i]$
		for $1\le j\le n$, and
		$y_\nu=(y_{\nu,1},\ldots,y_{\nu,d})\in\prod_{i=1}^d[-E_i,E_i]$
		for $\nu\in\mathcal I$.
		For $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and complex coefficients $b=(b_\nu)_{\nu\in\mathcal I}$
		with $|b_\nu|\le1$, put
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
			F_b(x)=\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal I}b_\nu e(x\cdot y_\nu),\qquad
			P=\prod_{i=1}^d(1+D_iE_i),\\
			B=\#\{(j,j')\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^2:
			|x_{j,i}-x_{j',i}|\le E_i^{-1}\ (1\le i\le d)\}.
		\end{gathered}
		\]
		For $q>2$, set $\mathcal A_q=\sup_{|b_\nu|\le1}
		\|F_b\|_{L^q_\#(\mathcal X)}$. For complex coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_n$
		with $|a_j|\le1$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:elementary-sieve}
			\left|\sum_{j=1}^na_jF_b(x_j)\right|
			\lesssim_{d,q}P^{1/q}n^{1-2/q}B^{1/q}\mathcal A_q.
		\end{equation}
		If $c_4,c_6\ge0$ satisfy, for every $\lambda>0$,
		\[
		\sup_{|b_\nu|\le1}
		\frac{|\{x\in\mathcal X:|F_b(x)|>\lambda\}|}{|\mathcal X|}
		\le c_4\lambda^{-4}+c_6\lambda^{-6},
		\]
		then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:distributional-sieve}
			\left|\sum_{j=1}^na_jF_b(x_j)\right|
			\lesssim_d\sum_{q\in\{4,6\}}P^{1/q}n^{1-2/q}B^{1/q}c_q^{1/q}.
		\end{equation}
		The count $B$ includes all ordered pairs of indices, with their multiplicities.
head: environment
name: Double large sieve

label: eq:sieve-amplitude-split
title: Proof
body_md:
The moment estimate \eqref{eq:elementary-sieve} is
		\cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.BW18}{Section~5}}, (5.5)]{BW18}, with bounded coefficients as in
		\cite[\mbox{\hyperlink{cite.BW18}{Section~9}}, (9.1)--(9.4)]{BW18}.
		For \eqref{eq:distributional-sieve}, partition $\mathcal X$ into
		axis-parallel boxes $\mathcal Q$ of side lengths
		\[
		\delta_i=\frac{2D_i}{\max\{1,\lceil2D_iE_i\rceil\}},\qquad
		\delta_iE_i\le1,\qquad |\mathcal Q|^{-1}\lesssim_d P/|\mathcal X|.
		\]
		Assign each $x_j$ to one box containing it, and let $n_{\mathcal Q}$ be the
		number of assigned indices. Then
		\[
		\sum_{\mathcal Q} n_{\mathcal Q}=n,\qquad \sum_{\mathcal Q}n_{\mathcal Q}^2\le B.
		\]
		Fix the coefficient sequence $b$.
		For $\mu\in\{0,1\}^d$, define
		\[
		F_{b,\mu}(x)=\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal I}b_\nu
		\prod_{i=1}^d(y_{\nu,i}/E_i)^{\mu_i}e(x\cdot y_\nu).
		\]
		These coefficients have modulus at most one. With
		$\partial^\mu=\partial_{x_1}^{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{x_d}^{\mu_d}$,
		\[
		\partial^\mu F_b=\left(\prod_{i=1}^d(2\pi\mathrm i E_i)^{\mu_i}\right)F_{b,\mu}.
		\]
		Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus in each coordinate gives,
		for $x_j\in \mathcal Q$,
		\[
		|F_b(x_j)|\le\frac1{|\mathcal Q|}\sum_{\mu\in\{0,1\}^d}
		\prod_{i=1}^d\delta_i^{\mu_i}\int_{\mathcal Q}|\partial^\mu F_b|
		\lesssim_d\frac1{|\mathcal Q|}\sum_{\mu\in\{0,1\}^d}\int_{\mathcal Q}|F_{b,\mu}|.
		\]
		For $\lambda>0$, integration of the distribution function gives
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\int_{\mathcal X\cap\{|F_{b,\mu}|>\lambda\}}|F_{b,\mu}|^2
			&=\lambda^2|\mathcal X\cap\{|F_{b,\mu}|>\lambda\}|
			+2\int_\lambda^\infty t|\mathcal X\cap\{|F_{b,\mu}|>t\}|\,dt\\
			&\lesssim|\mathcal X|\bigl(c_4\lambda^{-2}+c_6\lambda^{-4}\bigr).
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Split each integral over $\mathcal Q$ at $|F_{b,\mu}|=\lambda$ and use
		Cauchy--Schwarz. For every $\lambda>0$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:sieve-amplitude-split}
			\begin{split}
				\left|\sum_{j=1}^na_jF_b(x_j)\right|
				&\lesssim_d n\lambda+
				\left(\sum_{\mathcal Q}\frac{n_{\mathcal Q}^2}{|\mathcal Q|}\right)^{1/2}
				\sum_{\mu\in\{0,1\}^d}
				\left(\int_{\mathcal X\cap\{|F_{b,\mu}|>\lambda\}}
				|F_{b,\mu}|^2\right)^{1/2}\\
				&\lesssim_d n\lambda+(PB)^{1/2}
				\big(c_4\lambda^{-2}+c_6\lambda^{-4}\big)^{1/2}.
			\end{split}
		\end{equation}
		If $c_4=c_6=0$, let $\lambda\downarrow0$ in
		\eqref{eq:sieve-amplitude-split}. Otherwise take
		$\lambda=(PBc_4/n^2)^{1/4}+(PBc_6/n^2)^{1/6}>0$.
		For $q\in\{4,6\}$, $PBc_q\lambda^{2-q}\le n^2\lambda^2$,
		which proves \eqref{eq:distributional-sieve}.
